name: word-freq
axis: mixed map + string: tokenize a synthetic corpus and count word frequencies (read-modify-write upsert)
n: v=2000 vocabulary, d=4000 documents of k=20 words (Zipf-ish quadratic skew from a MINSTD LCG), r=120 tokenizing passes = 9.6M tokens, then a 2000-entry checksum scan
nPython: r=12 instead of 120 (10x fewer passes = 960k tokens); v/d/k unchanged, so the corpus and the distinct-word count are identical
notes: Tokenization is an explicit code-point scan + slice in ALL FOUR, not a library split — Python's `.split()` and JS's would be C/handwritten-assembly fast and would not be the same algorithm, and VL has no `split` at all (VL's whole string surface is `slice(i32,i32)`, `indexOf(string)`, `includes(string)`, `charCodeAt(i32)`, `+`, `[i]`, `.length`). Every token is a FRESH string, which is what a real tokenizer produces and what makes the map do real hashing instead of short-circuiting on pointer identity. The corpus is D separate document strings rather than one large string because VL's `s = s + x` accumulator is QUADRATIC (measured: 25k appends 0.56s, 50k 2.8s, 100k 19.7s, 200k >60s) so a single large corpus string is not constructible in VL. Upsert asymmetry: Rust's idiomatic `*freq.entry(w.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1` is ONE probe; VL and JS and Python all need two (`m[w] = (m[w] ?? 0) + 1`). VL cost decomposition at this size, measured: char scan alone 147ms, +slice 345ms, +map upsert 955ms — so the map upsert is ~64% and the slice ~21%. opt.vl boxes the counter in a struct so the common path is ONE probe; it measured a WASH (1238ms vs 1216ms), which is the useful negative result: VL's second probe is not the gap, the per-probe cost is.
